Abstract.

We introduce a poset of weighted hypergraphs on a fixed vertex set which has a remarkable property: the Möbius values of the intervals associated to any hypergraph give, up to sign, the coefficients of the hh-polynomial of its nestohedron. We exploit this relation to provide two new recurrence relations to compute hh-polynomials of nestohedra.

Key words and phrases: 
Hypergraphs, building sets, nestohedra, hh-polynomials, Möbius functions
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary: 06A07, 05C65, 52B05 Secondary: 52B12

1. Introduction

Building sets were introduced in the work of De Concini and Procesi on wonderful compactifications of complements of complex hyperplane arrangements [4]. They capture the notion of connectivity present in many mathematical contexts and have been generalized further from Boolean algebras to general semilattices in the work of Feichtner and Kozlov in [7].

A building set on ground set VV is a collection ℬ⊆𝒫⁡(V)\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(V) of nonempty subsets (blocks) of VV satisfying that

  1. (B1)

    if I,J∈ℬI,J\in\mathcal{B} and I∩J≠∅I\cap J\not=\emptyset, then I∪J∈ℬI\cup J\in\mathcal{B}.

  2. (B2)

    ℬ\mathcal{B} contains the singleton {v}\{v\}, for all v∈Vv\in V.

The most natural examples of building sets are perhaps the ones associated to connectivity in graphs. For a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) on vertex set VV and set of edges E=E⁡(G)E=E(G), the family ℬ⁡(G)\mathcal{B}(G) formed by subsets I⊆VI\subseteq V such that the induced subgraph of GG on vertex set II is connected, is a building set. Building sets of the form ℬ⁡(G)\mathcal{B}(G) are known as graphical.

In a greater generality, recall that a (multi) hypergraph HH on V=:V⁡(H)V=:V(H), is a collection of (possibly repeated) nonempty subsets of VV, called hyperedges, where any two hyperedges on the same underlying vertex set are considered to be distinct—to have different identities. For a hypergraph HH on VV, the collection ℬ⁡(H)\mathcal{B}(H) of subsets of VV that are connected by elements of HH (see Section 2 for the definition) also forms a building set. Every building set is of the form ℬ=ℬ⁡(H)\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{B}(H) for some hypergraph HH, but this map is not a bijection since there are infinitely many HH satisfing this property. In fact, we can consider building sets ℬ\mathcal{B} as hypergraphs themselves, and in such case—after an abuse of notation—ℬ=ℬ⁡(ℬ)\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{B}). However, as we argue later, ℬ\mathcal{B} is not the minimal hypergraph HH such that ℬ=ℬ⁡(H)\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{B}(H) as long as ℬ≠∅\mathcal{B}\neq\emptyset.

Starting from a building set ℬ\mathcal{B} on VV we can associate a polytope which captures its combinatorial information. Define the ℬ\mathcal{B}-nestohedron as the convex polytope PℬP_{\mathcal{B}} in ℝV\mathbb{R}^{V} defined by the Minkowsky sum

Pℬ:=∑I∈ℬΔI,P_{\mathcal{B}}:=\sum_{I\in\mathcal{B}}\Delta_{I},

where ΔI⊆ℝV\Delta_{I}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{V} is the convex hull of the standard basis vectors {𝒆v:v∈I}\{\boldsymbol{e}_{v}:v\in I\}—known as a standard simplex. For a hypergraph HH, we define PH:=Pℬ⁡(H)P_{H}:=P_{\mathcal{B}(H)}11 1 This polytope is combinatorially and normally equivalent to the definition of the hypergraph polytope associated to HH in [5].. Nestohedra were introduced independently by several authors, including Postnikov [11] and Feichtner and Sturmfels [6]. They are dual to the nested set complexes introduced by De Concini and Procesi in [4] (see also [15]). The particular subfamily of graphical nestohedra was studied by Carr and Devadoss under the name of graph-associahedra [3]. Figure 1 illustrates the ℬ0\mathcal{B}_{0}-nestohedron with building set

(1.1) ℬ0={{1},{2},{3},{4},{1,3},{2,3},{1,2,3},{1,2,4},{1,2,3,4}}.\mathcal{B}_{0}=\{\{1\},\{2\},\{3\},\{4\},\{1,3\},\{2,3\},\{1,2,3\},\{1,2,4\},\{1,2,3,4\}\}.

This polytope is 33-dimensional and all its vertices lie in the hyperplane x1+x2+x3+x4=5x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}+x_{4}=5.

To any polytope PP one can define its ff-polynomial by

fP​(t):=∑k≥0fk​tk,f_{P}(t):=\sum_{k\geq 0}f_{k}t^{k},

where fi=fi​(P)f_{i}=f_{i}(P) is the number of ii-dimensional faces of PP. A closely related polynomial is its hh-polynomial defined using the translation

hP​(t):=fP​(t−1).h_{P}(t):=f_{P}(t-1).

We denote by hH​(t):=hPH​(t)h_{H}(t):=h_{P_{H}}(t) the hh-polynomial of a hypergraph HH and by hℬ​(t)h_{\mathcal{B}}(t) the hh-polynomial of a building set ℬ\mathcal{B}. Note that by definition

hH​(t)=hℬ⁡(H)​(t).h_{H}(t)=h_{\mathcal{B}(H)}(t).

In our example, Figure 1 shows that fPℬ0​(t)=12+18​t+8​t2+t3f_{P_{\mathcal{B}_{0}}}(t)=12+18t+8t^{2}+t^{3}, and thus hℬ0​(t)=1+5​t+5​t2+t3h_{\mathcal{B}_{0}}(t)=1+5t+5t^{2}+t^{3}. In this article, we adopt the more general perspective of hypergraphs to study the hh-polynomials of their associated nestohedra.

The polytopes PHP_{H} are all simple, and hence their polar duals are simplicial. It follows then from a result of Bruggesser and Mani in [2] that their hh-polynomial has nonnegative integer coefficients. The fact that they are strictly positive and unimodal is a consequence of Stanley’s gg-theorem [13].

Postnikov, Reiner, and Williams proved in [10] that hℬ​(t)h_{\mathcal{B}}(t) can be computed as the descent enumerator of a family of rooted forests associated to ℬ\mathcal{B}, introduced by Postnikov in [11] under the name of ℬ\mathcal{B}-forests. This gives a combinatorial interpretation to the positive coefficients of hℬ​(t)h_{\mathcal{B}}(t). It is also shown in [10] that for a connected chordal building set ℬ\mathcal{B}, hℬ​(t)h_{\mathcal{B}}(t) can be computed as the descent enumerator of a family of permutations associated to ℬ\mathcal{B}, known as ℬ\mathcal{B}-permutations.

Using the recursive nature of the family of ℬ\mathcal{B}-forests, Postnikov derived a recursive characterization of ff- and hh-polynomials of nestohedra.

Proposition 1.1 (hh-version of Theorem 7.11 [11]).

The hh-polynomials associated to building sets are determined by the following recurrence relations:

  1. (1)

    If ℬ\mathcal{B} is the unique building set on a singleton, hℬ​(t)=1h_{\mathcal{B}}(t)=1.

  2. (2)

    If ℬ\mathcal{B} has connected components ℬ1,…,ℬk\mathcal{B}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{B}_{k}, then

    hℬ(t)=hℬ1(t)⋯hℬk(t).h_{\mathcal{B}}(t)=h_{\mathcal{B}_{1}}(t)\cdots h_{\mathcal{B}_{k}}(t).
  3. (3)

    If ℬ\mathcal{B} is connected, then

    hℬ​(t)=∑I⊊V(t−1)|V|−|I|−1​hℬ|I​(t),h_{\mathcal{B}}(t)=\sum_{I\subsetneq V}(t-1)^{|V|-|I|-1}h_{\mathcal{B}|_{I}}(t),

    where ℬ|I:={J∈ℬ∣J⊆I}\mathcal{B}|_{I}:=\{J\in\mathcal{B}\mid J\subseteq I\} is the restriction of ℬ\mathcal{B} to II, and by convention hℬ|∅​(t)=h∅​(t)=1h_{\mathcal{B}|_{\emptyset}}(t)=h_{\emptyset}(t)=1, for the vacuous case ℬ=∅\mathcal{B}=\emptyset on V=∅V=\emptyset.

Another recursion for the fℬ​(t)f_{\mathcal{B}}(t) was derived by Zelevinsky [15, Proposition 4.7] using a link decomposition of the nested set complex. The corresponding formula for hh-polynomials is as follows.

Proposition 1.2 (hh version of Proposition 4.7 [15]).

Let ℬ\mathcal{B} a building set on VV, then we have that

(n−κ(ℬ)−(t−1)dd​t)hℬ(t)=∑I∈ℬ∖ℬmaxhℬ|I(t)hI\ℬ(t),\left(n-\kappa(\mathcal{B})-(t-1)\frac{d}{dt}\right)h_{\mathcal{B}}(t)=\sum_{I\in\mathcal{B}\setminus\mathcal{B}_{\max}}h_{\mathcal{B}|_{I}}(t)h_{{}_{I}\backslash\mathcal{B}}(t),

where ℬmax\mathcal{B}_{\max} is the set of maximal blocks of ℬ\mathcal{B}, and \Iℬ={J⊆V∖I∣J∈ℬ or J∪I∈ℬ}.{}_{I}\backslash\mathcal{B}=\{J\subseteq V\setminus I\mid J\in\mathcal{B}\text{ or }J\cup I\in\mathcal{B}\}.22 2 We use a different notation here for I\ℬ{}_{I}\backslash\mathcal{B} than the one in [15] to avoid confusion with the definition of ℬ/𝒜\mathcal{B}/_{\mathcal{A}} that we use below.

The main goal of this work is to provide three new ways of computing hℬ​(t)h_{\mathcal{B}}(t) for any building set ℬ\mathcal{B}: one as a sum of the Möbius values on maximal intervals of a partially ordered set (poset for short), and a pair of recurrences based on the notion of spanning sub-building sets. All our formulas, which we prove in the general context of hypergraphs, are derived from our novel construction of the poset of weighted spanning hypergraphs 𝕎​ℍ​(V)\mathbb{WH}(V) on VV, see Definition 2.4.

We say that a hypergraph H′H^{\prime} is a spanning subhypergraph of a hypergraph HH if V⁡(H′)=V⁡(H)=VV(H^{\prime})=V(H)=V and H′⊆HH^{\prime}\subseteq H. This relation defines an order H′≤HH^{\prime}\leq H on the set of hypergraphs on VV. To define a corresponding order on building sets we rely on a stricter version of the inclusion for hypergraphs. Indeed, we define the relation with respect to the minimal generating subset of a building set under the properties (B1) and (B2).

Definition 1.3.

For a building set ℬ\mathcal{B} we denote by E⁡(ℬ)⊂ℬE(\mathcal{B})\subset\mathcal{B} the set of nonsingleton blocks S∈ℬS\in\mathcal{B}, such that whenever S=I∪JS=I\cup J for some I,J∈ℬI,J\in\mathcal{B} with I∩J≠∅I\cap J\neq\emptyset, we have I=SI=S or J=SJ=S. We call the elements of E⁡(ℬ)E(\mathcal{B}) the struts33 3 In [5] the authors call E⁡(ℬ)E(\mathcal{B}) a bare hypergraph. In this language, struts are the hyperedges of the underlying bare hypergraph. of ℬ\mathcal{B}.

For the building set ℬ0\mathcal{B}_{0} in (1.1) we illustrate E⁡(ℬ0)E(\mathcal{B}_{0}) in Figure 2.

The sets ℬ\mathcal{B} and E⁡(ℬ)E(\mathcal{B}) determine each other uniquely on V⁡(ℬ)V(\mathcal{B}), and hence we will consider ℬ\mathcal{B} and the pair (V⁡(ℬ),E⁡(ℬ))(V(\mathcal{B}),E(\mathcal{B})) indistinctly as the same object. This notation is inspired on the case of the graphical building set ℬ⁡(G)\mathcal{B}(G) of a simple graph GG where the struts are precisely the edges of GG, i.e., E⁡(G)=E⁡(ℬ⁡(G))E(G)=E(\mathcal{B}(G)). For a general hypergraph we define E⁡(H):=E⁡(ℬ⁡(H))E(H):=E(\mathcal{B}(H)). A consequence of this definition is that ℬ⁡(E⁡(H))=ℬ⁡(H)\mathcal{B}(E(H))=\mathcal{B}(H). Furthermore, PE⁡(ℬ)=PℬP_{E(\mathcal{B})}=P_{\mathcal{B}} and E⁡(ℬ)E(\mathcal{B}) is the minimal hypergraph with this property.

We define spanning sub-building sets as the natural generalization of spanning subgraphs of a simple graph, as follows.

Definition 1.4.

We say that a building set 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a spanning sub-building set of ℬ\mathcal{B} if E⁡(𝒜)E(\mathcal{A}) is a spanning subhypergraph of E⁡(ℬ)E(\mathcal{B}), i.e., if V⁡(𝒜)=V⁡(ℬ)V(\mathcal{A})=V(\mathcal{B}) and E⁡(𝒜)⊆E⁡(ℬ)E(\mathcal{A})\subseteq E(\mathcal{B}).

Remark 1.5.

A less strict, and perhaps more natural, notion of a spanning sub-building set can be defined whenever 𝒜⊆ℬ\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{B}. However, this notion differs from the one considered in this article. In particular, as we will show, a version of Theorem 1.7 below is true under the two notions, but the stricter condition results in recursive formulas with the least number of terms (see Proposition 5.1).

We consider the order relation 𝒜≤ℬ\mathcal{A}\leq\mathcal{B} whenever 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a spanning sub-building set of ℬ\mathcal{B}. Figure 3 shows the poset of building sets that lie below ℬ0\mathcal{B}_{0} from Figure 2. This poset is isomorphic to the Boolean algebra 𝔹E⁡(ℬ)\mathbb{B}_{E(\mathcal{B})} on E⁡(ℬ)E(\mathcal{B}).

We show that the Möbius values of the maximal intervals determined by weighted hypergraphs supported on HH, in the poset 𝕎​ℍ​(V)\mathbb{WH}(V) of Definition 2.4, give—up to sign—the coefficients of hH​(t)h_{H}(t).

Let HH be a hypergraph on VV. Then

In particular,

Finally, we use Theorem 1.6 to prove that the hh-polynomials of nestohedra can be computed using any of the next two recursions.

Theorem 1.7.

The hh-polynomials associated to building sets are determined by the following recurrence relations:

  1. (1)

    If ℬ\mathcal{B} consists of a singleton, hℬ​(t)=1h_{\mathcal{B}}(t)=1.

  2. (2)

    If ℬ\mathcal{B} has connected components ℬ1,…,ℬk\mathcal{B}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{B}_{k}, then

    hℬ(t)=hℬ1(t)⋯hℬk(t).h_{\mathcal{B}}(t)=h_{\mathcal{B}_{1}}(t)\cdots h_{\mathcal{B}_{k}}(t).
  3. (3)

    If ℬ\mathcal{B} is a connected building set with |V⁡(ℬ)|>1|V(\mathcal{B})|>1, then hℬ​(t)h_{\mathcal{B}}(t) satisfies the two recurrences:

    (1.3) hℬ​(t)=∑𝒜<ℬ(−1)|E⁡(ℬ)|−|E⁡(𝒜)|−1​[κ⁡(𝒜)]t​h𝒜​(t),\displaystyle h_{\mathcal{B}}(t)=\sum_{\mathcal{A}<\mathcal{B}}(-1)^{|E(\mathcal{B})|-|E(\mathcal{A})|-1}[\kappa(\mathcal{A})]_{t}h_{\mathcal{A}}(t),

    and

    (1.4) hℬ(t)=∑𝒜≤ℬE⁡(𝒜)≠∅(−1)|E⁡(𝒜)|−1hℬ/𝒜(t)∏I∈𝒜max[|I|]t,\displaystyle h_{\mathcal{B}}(t)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{A}\leq\mathcal{B}\\ E(\mathcal{A})\neq\emptyset\end{subarray}}(-1)^{|E(\mathcal{A})|-1}h_{\mathcal{B}/_{\mathcal{A}}}(t)\prod_{I\in\mathcal{A}_{\max}}[\,|I|\,]_{t},

    where ℬ/𝒜{\mathcal{B}/_{\mathcal{A}}} is the contraction of the building set ℬ\mathcal{B} by 𝒜\mathcal{A} (see Definition 2.2) and [n]t:=1+t+⋯+tn−1[n]_{t}:=1+t+\cdots+t^{n-1}.

Remark 1.8.

Comparing the recursion of Proposition 1.1 with the new recursions of Theorem 1.7, the reader may notice that they are fundamentally different and, in particular, involve a different number of terms. The latter requires fewer terms to be computed when applied to building sets ℬ\mathcal{B} satisfying |E⁡(ℬ)|<|V⁡(ℬ)||E(\mathcal{B})|<|V(\mathcal{B})|.

Remark 1.9.

A key application of (1.3) appears in [1] where we use this recurrence to extend and prove a conjectural relation, posed by the third author and Wachs in [8], between a new polynomial invariant of a graph (called the μ\mu-polynomial) and the hh-polynomial of its nestohedron.

This article is organized as follows: In Section 2 we introduce the poset 𝕎​ℍ​(V)\mathbb{WH}(V) of weighted hypergraphs on vertex set VV, describe some of its structural properties and prove some relations satisfied by its Möbius function. The proofs of Theorems 1.6 and 1.7 in Section 5 rely on the concept of a ℬ\mathcal{B}-forest, which we extend to define HH-forests and discuss some of its equivalent definitions in Section 3. The main results also depend on the auxiliary Proposition 4.1 whose proof relies on a judicious sign-reversing involution, which we construct in Section 4. We conclude in Section 6 with two examples using Theorem 1.7 to compute the hh-polynomials of two infinite families of nestohedra.

2. The poset of weighted hypergraphs

In this section we introduce the poset of weighted hypergraphs and derive some properties of its Möbius function. Moreover, we study the auxiliary polynomial MH​(t)M_{H}(t) given by the left-hand side of (1.2) and develop its main properties. This will be essential in the proof of Theorem 1.6. We refer the reader to [12, 14] for undefined terminology and results concerning posets.

2.1. Hypergraphs and connectivity

Formally, a hypergraph HH on V=:V⁡(H)V=:V(H) is a collection of pairs 𝖨=(I,i)∈H\mathsf{I}=(I,i)\in H, called hyperedges, where ∅≠I⊆V\emptyset\neq I\subseteq V and ii is any label that makes the pair unique in HH. We consider two hyperedges (I,i)(I,i) and (J,j)(J,j) as different if either I≠JI\neq J or i≠ji\neq j, and we denote by V⁡(𝖨):=IV(\mathsf{I}):=I the underlying vertex set of 𝖨\mathsf{I}. If there is a single hyperedge 𝖨=(I,i)\mathsf{I}=(I,i) with vertex set I⊆V⁡(H)I\subseteq V(H), we can abuse notation and ignore its label, denoting such hyperedge simply by II. Building sets ℬ\mathcal{B}, and more generally hypergraphs without repeated hyperedges, can be considered as hypergraphs—I∈ℬI\in\mathcal{B} can, for example, be viewed as the hyperedge (I,I)(I,I), with underlying set II and label II.

For any hypergraph HH on VV and ∅≠I⊆V\emptyset\neq I\subseteq V we define the restriction of HH to II as the hypergraph on vertex set II and hyperedges given by

H|I={𝖩∣V⁡(𝖩)⊆I}.H|_{I}=\{\mathsf{J}\mid V(\mathsf{J})\subseteq I\}.

We say that I⊆VI\subseteq V is connected by HH if there is no nontrivial bipartition (separation) I=A⊔BI=A\sqcup B such that H|I=H|A⊔H|BH|_{I}=H|_{A}\sqcup H|_{B}. The set HmaxH_{\max} consists of the inclusion-maximal subsets of VV connected by HH. The elements in HmaxH_{\max} are pairwise disjoint and form a partition of VV. The connected components of HH are the restrictions H|IH|_{I}, for each I∈HmaxI\in H_{\max}. We write κ⁡(H)=|Hmax|\kappa(H)=|H_{\max}| and we say that HH is connected whenever Hmax={V}H_{\max}=\{V\}—and hence κ⁡(H)=1\kappa(H)=1.

The collection

ℬ⁡(H)={I⊆V∣H|I​ is connected}\mathcal{B}(H)=\{I\subseteq V\mid H|_{I}\text{ is connected}\}

forms a building set and, as we mentioned in Section 1, every building set ℬ\mathcal{B} is of this form.

2.2. Contraction and dispensable hyperedges

We define the contraction of a hypergraph by a spanning subhypergraph.

Definition 2.1.

Given H′≤HH^{\prime}\leq H we define the contraction H/H′H/_{H^{\prime}} as the hypergraph on vertex set V(H/H′)=Hmax′V(H/_{H^{\prime}})=H^{\prime}_{\max} and hyperedges given by

(2.1) H/H′={({I∈Hmax′∣I∩V(𝖩)≠∅},𝖩)|𝖩∈H∖H′}.H/_{H^{\prime}}=\bigg\{\bigg(\{I\in H^{\prime}_{\max}\mid I\cap V(\mathsf{J})\neq\emptyset\},\mathsf{J}\bigg)\,\bigg|\,\mathsf{J}\in H\setminus H^{\prime}\bigg\}.

In particular, |H/H′|=|H|−|H|′|H/_{H^{\prime}}|=|H|-|H|^{\prime}.

Note that the restriction operation is defined similarly for hypergraphs and for building sets, since both families are closed under the same restriction. In contrast, these families are not closed under (2.1). Indeed, even when HH does not have multiple hyperedges, singleton hyperedges, or non-strut hyperedges, all three cases may appear in a contraction H/H′H/_{H^{\prime}}. Therefore contraction must be defined slightly differently for building sets.

We say that two hypergraphs HH and H′H^{\prime} are isomorphic if there is a bijection f:V⁡(H)→V⁡(H′)f:V(H)\to V(H^{\prime}) such that for every I⊆VI\subseteq V, we have that

|{𝖨∈H∣V⁡(𝖨)=I}|=|{𝖩∈H′∣V⁡(𝖩)=f⁡(I)}|,|\{\mathsf{I}\in H\mid V(\mathsf{I})=I\}|=|\{\mathsf{J}\in H^{\prime}\mid V(\mathsf{J})=f(I)\}|,

i.e., the number of hyperedges in HH with underlying vertex set II is the same as the number of hyperedges in H′H^{\prime} with underlying vertex set f⁡(I)f(I).

Following a similar idea as in [5], we say that 𝖩∈H\mathsf{J}\in H is dispensable in HH when H|V⁡(𝖩)∖𝖩H|_{V(\mathsf{J})}\setminus\mathsf{J} is connected. In the language of [5], a bare hypergraph is a hypergraph without dispensable hyperedges. Note that for a hypergraph HH, E⁡(H)E(H) coincides with any representative of the isomorphism class of the hypergraphs obtained after a one-by-one removal of dispensable elements at each step. It follows that the resulting hypergraphs are all isomorphic, independently of the order of the dispensable hyperedges removed at each step. In particular, their hyperedges can be regarded as having no labels.

Definition 2.2.

For building sets 𝒜\mathcal{A} and ℬ\mathcal{B} such that 𝒜≤ℬ\mathcal{A}\leq\mathcal{B}, i.e., E⁡(𝒜)⊆E⁡(ℬ)E(\mathcal{A})\subseteq E(\mathcal{B}), we define the contracted building set ℬ/𝒜\mathcal{B}/_{\mathcal{A}} as the building set associated to the contracted hypergraph ℬ/𝒜\mathcal{B}/_{\mathcal{A}}, with ℬ\mathcal{B} and 𝒜\mathcal{A} regarded as hypergraphs.

A consequence of Definition 2.2 is that the struts of ℬ/𝒜\mathcal{B}/_{\mathcal{A}} can be obtained from either hypergraph contractions ℬ/𝒜\mathcal{B}/_{\mathcal{A}} or E(ℬ)/E⁡(𝒜)E(\mathcal{B})/_{E(\mathcal{A})}, after removing all dispensable hyperedges. The following example illustrates Definitions 2.1 and 2.2.

Example 2.3.

Consider the two hypergraphs on [9][9]

A weighted hypergraph on VV is a pair 𝑯=(H,w𝑯)\boldsymbol{H}=(H,w_{\boldsymbol{H}}) where HH is a hypergraph on VV and w𝑯:Hmax→ℕw_{\boldsymbol{H}}:H_{\max}\rightarrow\mathbb{N} is a weight function that assigns a value 0≤w𝑯​(I)<|I|0\leq w_{\boldsymbol{H}}(I)<|I|, for every I∈HmaxI\in H_{\max}.

3. On ℬ\mathcal{B}-forests and HH-forests

It was shown in [10] that hh-polynomials of nestohedra admit a combinatorial interpretation in terms of a family of rooted forests introduced in [11], known as ℬ\mathcal{B}-forests. In this section, we recall this notion in the language of hypergraphs. Recall that the collection of subsets of VV that are connected in a hypergraph HH on VV forms a building set ℬ⁡(H)\mathcal{B}(H), and that this map is not injective. For a hypergraph HH the notion of HH-forest below coincides with the notion of ℬ⁡(H)\mathcal{B}(H)-forest in [11]. These objects are also in bijective correspondence with maximal nested sets in [4] and with constructions in [5].

Recall that a rooted forest is a forest in which a distinguished node (a root) is selected in each connected component (tree). For a rooted forest FF, given two nodes uu and vv of FF, we say that uu is a descendant of vv if vv belongs to the shortest path connecting uu with the root of its connected component. We denote the set of descendants of vv in FF by F≤vF_{\leq v}. Note that v∈F≤vv\in F_{\leq v}. Moreover, if FF has roots r1,…,rMr_{1},\dots,r_{M}, the sets of vertices of the connected components of FF form the partition Fmax:={F≤r1,…,F≤rM}F_{\max}:=\{F_{\leq_{r_{1}}},\dots,F_{\leq_{r_{M}}}\} of VV.

A descendant uu of vv is called a child of vv if uu is a descendant of vv and (u,v)∈E⁡(F)(u,v)\in E(F). Finally, we say that uu and vv are incomparable in FF if neither uu is a descendant of vv, nor vv is a descendant of uu.

Definition 3.1 (c.f. Definition 7.7, [11]).

A rooted forest FF on VV is an HH-forest for a hypergraph HH on VV when

  1. (HF1)

    For every v∈Vv\in V, H|F≤vH|_{F_{\leq v}} is connected.

  2. (HF2)

    For any incomparable nodes u1,…,uku_{1},\dots,u_{k} in FF, k≥2k\geq 2, H|⋃j=1kF≤ujH|_{\bigcup_{j=1}^{k}F_{\leq u_{j}}} is not connected.

  3. (HF3)

    We have that Fmax=HmaxF_{\max}=H_{\max}.

The connected components of an HH-forest are called HH-trees, each of which is associated with a connected component of HH.

Remark 3.2.

Given a hypergraph HH, the previous conditions can be expressed in terms of the corresponding building set ℬ⁡(H)\mathcal{B}(H) as follows. (HF1) asks that F≤v∈ℬ⁡(H)F_{\leq v}\in\mathcal{B}(H), for all v∈Vv\in V. (HF2) means that ⋃j=1kF≤uj∉ℬ⁡(H)\bigcup_{j=1}^{k}F_{\leq u_{j}}\not\in\mathcal{B}(H), for incomparable nodes u1,…,uku_{1},\dots,u_{k}. Finally, (HF3) says that Fmax=ℬ​(H)maxF_{\max}=\mathcal{B}(H)_{\max}.

This shows that if ℬ=ℬ⁡(H1)=ℬ⁡(H2)\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{B}(H_{1})=\mathcal{B}(H_{2}) for hypergraphs H1H_{1} and H2H_{2}, the H1H_{1}-forests and H2H_{2}-forests are the same, and are simply the ℬ\mathcal{B}-forests defined in [11].

The following is a recursive description of HH-trees originally presented in [11] in terms of ℬ⁡(H)\mathcal{B}(H)-trees.

Proposition 3.3 (cf. Proposition 8.5, [10]).

Consider a connected hypergraph HH on VV, v∈Vv\in V, and let H1,…,HkH_{1},\dots,H_{k} be the connected components of the restricted hypergraph H|V∖vH|_{V\setminus v}. Then all the HH-trees TT with root vv are obtained recursively by connecting to vv the roots of HiH_{i}-trees TiT_{i} for i=1,…,ki=1,\dots,k.

Therefore, moving through all the possible values of v∈Vv\in V in Proposition 3.3 we obtain all HH-trees. When HH is not connected, we apply this process to each of its connected components to construct all HH-forests of HH.

Example 3.4.

Consider the hypergraph HH and the tree TT given in Figure 6. By taking v=1v=1, HH restricted to {2,…,8}\{2,\dots,8\} leaves a hypergraph with three connected components H1={({2,3},i),({2,3},i​i)}H_{1}=\{(\{2,3\},i),(\{2,3\},ii)\}, H2={{4,6}H_{2}=\{\{4,6\}, {6}}\{6\}\} and H3={{5,7},{5,7,8},({7},a),({7},b)}H_{3}=\{\{5,7\},\{5,7,8\},(\{7\},a),(\{7\},b)\}. Removing v=1v=1 from TT gives a forest with three trees. The reader can verify that these trees correspond to HjH_{j}-trees for each of Hj,j=1,2,3H_{j},j=1,2,3. Therefore, TT is an HH-tree.

For the arguments below, we restate Proposition 3.3 in the following form.

Lemma 3.5.

Let HH be a hypergraph and FF a rooted forest on VV. Then FF is an HH-forest if and only if Fmax=HmaxF_{\max}=H_{\max} and for a root rr of FF, F|V∖rF|_{V\setminus r} is an H|V∖rH|_{V\setminus r}-forest.

Given a hypergraph HH and v∈V⁡(H)v\in V(H), we will denote by

Hv={𝖨∈H|v∈V⁡(𝖨)}⊆H,H_{v}=\{\mathsf{I}\in H\ |\ v\in V(\mathsf{I})\}\subseteq H,

the set of hyperedges of HH containing vv.

Remark 3.6.

Note that H=⋃v∈V⁡(H)HvH=\bigcup_{v\in V(H)}H_{v}. Moreover, if |V|>1|V|>1 and HH is connected, we see that Hv≠∅H_{v}\not=\emptyset for all v∈V⁡(H)v\in V(H).

Furthermore, Proposition 3.3 shows that HH-forests induce a natural decomposition of HH as follows.

Lemma 3.7.

Let HH be a hypergraph on VV and let FF be an HH-forest with roots r0=r,…,rm∈Vr_{0}=r,\dots,r_{m}\in V.

  1. (1)

    If 𝖨∈H\mathsf{I}\in H and V⁡(𝖨)∩F≤r≠∅V(\mathsf{I})\cap F_{\leq r}\neq\emptyset, then V⁡(𝖨)⊆F≤rV(\mathsf{I})\subseteq F_{\leq r}. In particular, Hr⊆H|F≤rH_{r}\subseteq H|_{F_{\leq_{r}}}, and H=H|F≤r0⊔⋯⊔H|F≤rmH=H|_{F_{\leq_{r_{0}}}}\sqcup\dots\sqcup H|_{F_{\leq_{r_{m}}}}, as a disjoint union.

  2. (2)

    If HH is connected and u1,…,ulu_{1},\dots,u_{l} are the children of rr in FF, then

    H=Hr⊔⨆i=1lH|F≤ui,H=H_{r}\sqcup\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{l}H|_{F_{\leq_{u_{i}}}},

    as a disjoint union.

Proof.

If V⁡(𝖨)⊈F≤rV(\mathsf{I})\not\subseteq F_{\leq r}, V⁡(𝖨)∪F≤rV(\mathsf{I})\cup F_{\leq r} is a larger set connected by HH contradicting (HF3), so V⁡(𝖨)⊆F≤rV(\mathsf{I})\subseteq F_{\leq r}. The other statements follow from this property. ∎

For the following result we consider that VV is provided with the structure of a total order VV. For instance, if V=[n]V=[n] we can use the usual order of the integers. Assuming this order, we can say that an edge (u,v)∈E⁡(F)(u,v)\in E(F), in an HH-forest FF, is a descent if u>vu>v. The total number of descents in FF is denoted des​(F)\textup{des}(F).

Proposition 3.8 (c.f. Corollary 8.4, [10]).

If HH is a hypergraph on an ordered set VV, then

hH​(t)=∑F​ an ​H​-forest tdes​(F).h_{H}(t)=\sum_{F\text{ an }H\text{-forest }}t^{\textup{des}(F)}.

Naturally, if ℬ=ℬ⁡(H)\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{B}(H), for some HH, this sum over the HH-forests is the same as the sum over the ℬ\mathcal{B}-forests, which is consistent with our definition hH​(t)=hℬ⁡(H)​(t)h_{H}(t)=h_{\mathcal{B}(H)}(t).

4. A sign reversing involution

The goal of this section is to establish an analogous equation to (2.8) for hh-polynomials of hypergraphs. More precisely, we prove the following.

Proposition 4.1.

Let HH be a connected hypergraph such that |V⁡(H)|>1|V(H)|>1. Then

(4.1) ∑H′≤H[κ⁡(H′)]t​(−1)|H′|​hH′​(t)=0.\sum_{H^{\prime}\leq H}[\kappa(H^{\prime})]_{t}(-1)^{|H^{\prime}|}h_{H^{\prime}}(t)=0.

The idea is to rewrite (4.1) as a sum over a suitable set of combinatorial objects ΩH\Omega_{H} together with a weight function ω:ΩH→ℤ⁡[t]\omega:\Omega_{H}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}[t]. We want ω⁡(x)\omega(x) to be the contribution of x∈ΩHx\in\Omega_{H} to the left-hand side of (4.1). Then, we find a sign-reversing involution ψ:ΩH→ΩH,\psi:\Omega_{H}\to\Omega_{H}, i.e., ψ∘ψ=idΩH\psi\circ\psi=\text{id}_{\Omega_{H}} and ω⁡(ψ⁡(x))=−ω⁡(x)\omega(\psi(x))=-\omega(x), and conclude that the left-hand side of (4.1) vanishes.

Based on Proposition 3.8, we can replace the polynomial hH′​(t)h_{H^{\prime}}(t), by the sum of tdes​(F)t^{\textup{des}(F)} over all H′H^{\prime}-forest FF. Moreover, if FF is an H′H^{\prime}-forest, we can sort its roots

r0<r1<⋯<rκ⁡(H′)−1r_{0}<r_{1}<\cdots<r_{\kappa(H^{\prime})-1}

in ascending order, according to the total order of VV and define σF​(ri):=i\sigma_{F}(r_{i}):=i.

Lemma 4.6.

The map ψ\psi in (4.3) is a sign-reversing involution on ΩH\Omega_{H}.

Proof.

Lemma 4.5 (1) and (2) show that ψ⁡(H′,F,r)∈ΩH\psi(H^{\prime},F,r)\in\Omega_{H}, for all (H′,F,r)∈ΩH(H^{\prime},F,r)\in\Omega_{H}, so ψ\psi is well-defined. The fact that ψ∘ψ=idΩH\psi\circ\psi=\text{id}_{\Omega_{H}} is a direct consequence of Lemma 4.5(3). Let us write ψ⁡(H′,F,r)=(H′′,F′,r)\psi(H^{\prime},F,r)=(H^{\prime\prime},F^{\prime},r).

To prove that ψ\psi is sign reversing, we need to show that

5. Proofs of Theorems 1.6 and 1.7

These results will follow from the next analogue of Theorem 1.7, where hh-polynomials are indexed by hypergraphs and computed recursively.

Proposition 5.1.

The hh-polynomials associated to hypergraphs are determined by the following recurrence relations:

  1. (1)

    If H=∅H=\emptyset, hH​(t)=1h_{H}(t)=1.

  2. (2)

    If HH has connected components H1,…,HkH_{1},\dots,H_{k}, then

    hH(t)=hH1(t)⋯hHk(t).h_{H}(t)=h_{H_{1}}(t)\cdots h_{H_{k}}(t).
  3. (3)

    If HH is a connected hypergraph with |V⁡(H)|>1|V(H)|>1, then hH​(t)h_{H}(t) satisfies the two recurrences:

    (5.1) hH​(t)=∑H′<H(−1)|H|−|H′|−1​[κ⁡(H′)]t​hH′​(t),\displaystyle h_{H}(t)=\sum_{H^{\prime}<H}(-1)^{|H|-|H^{\prime}|-1}[\kappa(H^{\prime})]_{t}h_{H^{\prime}}(t),

    and

    (5.2) hH(t)=∑∅≠H′≤H(−1)|H′|−1hH/H′(t)∏I∈Hmax′[|I|]t.\displaystyle h_{H}(t)=\sum_{\emptyset\neq H^{\prime}\leq H}(-1)^{|H^{\prime}|-1}h_{H/_{H^{\prime}}}(t)\prod_{I\in H^{\prime}_{\max}}[\,|I|\,]_{t}.
Proof.

Formulas (1) and (2) are valid thanks to Proposition 1.1, and (5.1) follows from Proposition 4.1 by solving for hH​(t)h_{H}(t). Therefore, the family {hH}\{h_{H}\} of hh-polynomials of hypergraphs is completely determined by (1), (2) and (5.1). But Propositions 2.7 shows that the same recurrences are satisfied by the family of auxiliary polynomials {MH}\{M_{H}\}. By uniqueness, we see that

(5.3) (−1)|H|​hH​(t)=MH​(t),for all hypergraphs ​H.(-1)^{|H|}h_{H}(t)=M_{H}(t),\qquad\text{for all hypergraphs }H.

Finally, (5.2) follows from (2.9) by using (5.3) and solving for hHh_{H} which corresponds to H′=∅H^{\prime}=\emptyset. Note that here we used that |H/H′|=|H|−|H′||H/_{H^{\prime}}|=|H|-|H^{\prime}| and that H/∅H/_{\emptyset} is isomorphic to HH. ∎

The previous proof includes the proof of Theorem 1.6, which is exactly (5.3). Moreover, Theorem 1.7 is a particular case of Proposition 5.1. Indeed, if ℬ\mathcal{B} is a connected building set, E⁡(ℬ)E(\mathcal{B}) is a connected hypergraph. Now, if H′≤E⁡(ℬ)H^{\prime}\leq E(\mathcal{B}), then H′H^{\prime} is of the form H′=E⁡(𝒜)H^{\prime}=E(\mathcal{A}), for a unique spanning sub-building set 𝒜≤ℬ\mathcal{A}\leq\mathcal{B}. Moreover, H′H^{\prime} and 𝒜\mathcal{A} have the same number of connected components. Therefore, (5.1) gives (1.3) when applied to H=E⁡(ℬ)H=E(\mathcal{B}) since hH​(t)=hE⁡(ℬ)​(t)=hℬ​(t)h_{H}(t)=h_{E(\mathcal{B})}(t)=h_{\mathcal{B}}(t). In the same way, (5.2) gives (1.4) since by Definition 2.2 the struts of the building set ℬ/𝒜\mathcal{B}/_{\mathcal{A}} coincide with E(E(ℬ)/E⁡(𝒜))E(E(\mathcal{B})/_{E(\mathcal{A})}) for the contracted hypergraph E(ℬ)/E⁡(𝒜)E(\mathcal{B})/_{E(\mathcal{A})}. Thus hℬ/𝒜(t)=hE(ℬ/𝒜)(t)=hE(E(ℬ)/E⁡(𝒜))(t)=hE(ℬ)/E⁡(𝒜)(t)h_{\mathcal{B}/_{\mathcal{A}}}(t)=h_{E(\mathcal{B}/_{\mathcal{A}})}(t)=h_{E(E(\mathcal{B})/_{E(\mathcal{A})})}(t)=h_{E(\mathcal{B})/_{E(\mathcal{A})}}(t), giving the required recursion.

Corollary 5.2.

For any two hypergraphs H,H′H,H^{\prime} on VV with ℬ⁡(H)=ℬ⁡(H′)\mathcal{B}(H)=\mathcal{B}(H^{\prime}), we have that

(−1)|H|​MH​(t)=(−1)|H′|​MH′​(t).(-1)^{|H|}M_{H}(t)=(-1)^{|H^{\prime}|}M_{H^{\prime}}(t).

In particular,

hH​(t)=(−1)|H|​MH​(t)=(−1)|E⁡(H)|​ME⁡(H)​(t)=(−1)|ℬ⁡(H)|​Mℬ⁡(H)​(t).h_{H}(t)=(-1)^{|H|}M_{H}(t)=(-1)^{|E(H)|}M_{E(H)}(t)=(-1)^{|\mathcal{B}(H)|}M_{\mathcal{B}(H)}(t).

6. Examples

We illustrate the use of Theorem 1.7 with two examples. The strength of the new recursion can be appreciated in the cases where |E⁡(ℬ)|<|V⁡(ℬ)||E(\mathcal{B})|<|V(\mathcal{B})|.

Example 6.1.

Consider the building set

ℬn:={{i}∣i∈[n]}∪{[n]},\mathcal{B}_{n}:=\{\{i\}\mid i\in[n]\}\cup\{[n]\},

with ground set [n][n] and only strut [n][n], so PℬnP_{\mathcal{B}_{n}} is an (n−1)(n-1)-simplex. If 𝒜<ℬn\mathcal{A}<\mathcal{B}_{n}, then E⁡(𝒜)=∅E(\mathcal{A})=\emptyset and |κ⁡(A)|=n|\kappa(A)|=n. Therefore, we obtain directly from recurrence (1.3) that

hℬn​(t)=(−1)1−0−1​[n]t=[n]t,h_{\mathcal{B}_{n}}(t)=(-1)^{1-0-1}[n]_{t}=[n]_{t},

which gives a short proof of this well-known result, see [10, Example 6.11].

Example 6.2.

Fix integers 0≤k≤n0\leq k\leq n and consider the building set 𝒯n,k\mathcal{T}_{n,k} with ground set [n+k][n+k] and struts {l,l+n},l=1,…,k\{l,l+n\},l=1,\dots,k and [n][n], see Figure 9 for some examples. Note that if k=0k=0 we simply have 𝒯n,0=ℬn\mathcal{T}_{n,0}=\mathcal{B}_{n}.

In order to compute h𝒯n,kh_{\mathcal{T}_{n,k}} from (1.3) we describe all A≤𝒯n,kA\leq\mathcal{T}_{n,k}. There are two possibilities. First, [n]∈E⁡(𝒜)[n]\in E(\mathcal{A}). In this case, having 𝒜\mathcal{A} means choosing 0≤j≤k0\leq j\leq k lines to remove, thus |E⁡(𝒜)|=k−j+1|E(\mathcal{A})|=k-j+1, κ⁡(𝒜)=j+1\kappa(\mathcal{A})=j+1, and h𝒜=h𝒯n,k−jh_{\mathcal{A}}=h_{\mathcal{T}_{n,k-j}}. Second, if [n]∉E⁡(𝒜)[n]\not\in E(\mathcal{A}), removing 0≤j≤k0\leq j\leq k lines we have that |E⁡(𝒜)|=k−j|E(\mathcal{A})|=k-j, κ⁡(𝒜)=(k−j)+2​j+(n−k)=n+j\kappa(\mathcal{A})=(k-j)+2j+(n-k)=n+j, and h𝒜=hP2k−j=(1+t)k−jh_{\mathcal{A}}=h_{P_{2}}^{k-j}=(1+t)^{k-j}. In conclusion, (1.3) leads to the equation

∑j=0k(kj)​(−1)k−j+1​[j+1]t​h𝒯n,k−j​(t)+∑j=0k(kj)​(−1)k−j​[n+j]t​(1+t)k−j=0.\sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom{k}{j}(-1)^{k-j+1}{[j+1]_{t}}h_{\mathcal{T}_{n,k-j}}(t)+\sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom{k}{j}(-1)^{k-j}{[n+j]_{t}}(1+t)^{k-j}=0.

Let us write this as

∑j=0k(kj)​[j+1]t​(−1)k−j​h𝒯n,k−j​(t)=∑j=0k(kj)​[n+j]t​(−1)k−j​(1+t)k−j, 0≤k≤n.\sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom{k}{j}{[j+1]_{t}}(-1)^{k-j}h_{\mathcal{T}_{n,k-j}}(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom{k}{j}{[n+j]_{t}}{(-1)^{k-j}(1+t)^{k-j}},\,0\leq k\leq n.

Setting T⁡(t,z)=∑j=0n(−1)j​h𝒯n,j​(t)​zjj!T(t,z)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}(-1)^{j}h_{\mathcal{T}_{n,j}}(t)\frac{z^{j}}{j!} and using the exponential generating series

For instance, we have the values
